lessons.title: Why Some Leaders Inspire and Others Don't
lessons.key_idea: Great leaders and organizations like Apple stand out not because of what they make but because they communicate their purpose first.

lessons.title: The Golden Circle: Why, How, What
lessons.key_idea: Inspiring communication moves from the inside out, starting with why, then how, then what, while most organizations do the reverse.

lessons.title: Manipulation Works, But Only Briefly
lessons.key_idea: Price cuts, promotions, fear and novelty can drive sales, but they buy transactions rather than loyalty and grow costly over time.

lessons.title: It's Biology, Not Soft Talk
lessons.key_idea: The Golden Circle mirrors the brain, where the limbic system drives feelings and decisions, which is why a clear why can feel right before we can explain it.

lessons.title: Clarity, Discipline and Consistency
lessons.key_idea: A why only works when it is clear, guides how you act with discipline, and shows up consistently in everything you do, which builds trust.

lessons.title: Win the Early Adopters First
lessons.key_idea: Following the Law of Diffusion of Innovations, ideas spread when they first win the small group who share your beliefs, not when you chase the mass market directly.

lessons.title: When the Why Goes Fuzzy
lessons.key_idea: As organizations grow, the why can fade into a focus on results, so leaders must keep purpose clear, as in Sinek's account of Walmart after Sam Walton.

plan.title: Start With Why
plan.author: Simon Sinek
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's core framework, main arguments and signature examples well, including the Golden Circle, Apple, the Wright brothers, and the Law of Diffusion of Innovations.
plan.one_liner: People don't buy what you do. They buy why you do it. Here's what that changes.
plan.summary: Simon Sinek asks why some leaders and organizations, like Apple, Southwest Airlines and Martin Luther King Junior, inspire loyalty while others with similar resources do not. His answer is a simple model he calls the Golden Circle. Most organizations communicate from the outside in. They start with what they do, then how they do it, and rarely say why. Inspiring leaders reverse the order and start with their purpose. Sinek argues this works because it speaks to the part of the brain that drives feelings and decisions. He contrasts short-term manipulation, like discounts and promotions, with lasting inspiration built on trust. He shows how a clear why attracts early believers who carry ideas into the mainstream. He also warns that organizations lose their way when growth makes the why fuzzy.
